title: Spelling
summary: Two spelling items per shift, and they come from a predictable trap list: i/e flip-flops, double-letter failures, suffix endings and 90+ famous misspells. A rules layer (c-test, stress-doubling, keep-e) plus a weekly revised bank makes these near-guaranteed marks — the fastest scoring topic in Tier 1 English.

subtopics.title: i before e — and the exceptions that fill the paper
subtopics.concept:
**The rule:** write *i* before *e* when both spell the long 'ee' sound (bel**ie**ve, ach**ie**ve, gr**ie**f, f**ie**ld, sh**ie**ld); after the letter **c**, flip it — *e* before *i* (re**cei**ve, de**cei**ve, per**cei**ve, con**cei**ve, **cei**ling). Extended mnemonic: *i before e except after c, or when sounded like 'ay' as in neighbour and weigh* (n**ei**ghbour, w**ei**gh, **ei**ght). Height is different: its 'ei' sounds like 'eye', and it is simply an exception.

**But the SSC paper lives in the exceptions.** The high-frequency exceptions are: **weird, seize, height, foreign, sovereign, leisure, either, neither, their, counterfeit, protein** — memorise as a 10-word list; they appear as options constantly.

**i/e and e/i words**

| Correct | Trap spelling | Hook |
|---|---|---|
| **believe** | ~~beleive~~ | i before e when it rhymes with 'long e' (bel-eve) |
| **achieve** | ~~acheive~~ | same rule: -ieve |
| **friend** | ~~freind~~ | exception remembered as: fr-I-End — it ends with END |
| **mischief** | ~~mischeif~~ | short-i sound, still ie: -mischief |
| **receive** | ~~recieve~~ | after c the order flips: e before i |
| **deceive** | ~~decieve~~ | c + eive |
| **perceive** | ~~percieve~~ | c + eive |
| **conceive** | ~~concieve~~ | c + eive |
| **ceiling** | ~~cieling~~ | c + eiling |
| **ceiling fan** | ~~cieling fan~~ | the c governs: ei |
| **weird** | ~~wierd~~ | famous exception: ei, no c needed |
| **seize** | ~~sieze~~ | exception: seize the ei |
| **height** | ~~hieght~~ | exception: h-eight (compare weight) |
| **weight** | ~~waight~~ | ei like height — they rhyme and match |
| **foreign** | ~~foriegn~~ | exception: foreign keeps ei |
| **sovereign** | ~~soveriegn~~ | same family as foreign: -reign |
| **leisure** | ~~liesure~~ | exception: lei-sure |
| **either** | ~~iether~~ | ei family |
| **neither** | ~~niether~~ | ei family |
| **their** | ~~thier~~ | possessive of they: ei (th-eir) |

**Exam shape:** four spellings of the same word, one letter shifted. Read the options letter by letter — the difference is almost always one vowel pair: recieve/receive, wierd/weird. If the word follows 'c', demand 'ei'; if it doesn't, demand 'ie' — then check the exception list.

tricks.title: The c-test
tricks.body: Is there a c right before the pair? c → 'ei' (receive). No c → usually 'ie' (believe). Ten exceptions override: weird, seize, height, foreign, sovereign, leisure, either, neither, their, protein.

tricks.title: Rhyme-anchor pairs
tricks.body: height–weight rhyme and must match; believe–achieve match; receive–deceive match. Fix one of each pair forever and its partner comes free.

tricks.title: Say it in syllables
tricks.body: Pronounce the word slowly in your head — be-lieve, re-ceive. The mouth half-confirms what the eye doubts.

mistakes: Applying the rule to 'height' and writing 'hieght' — it is on the exception list.
Writing 'sciense' — after c comes 'ie' here only because the c is in 'sci' pronounced 's' + long i: memorise con-science = con + science.
Missing that 'friend' is ie, not ei — it does not rhyme with 'long e' but the spelling is still ie.
Trusting sound alone: 'receve' sounds right but has lost the i entirely.
subtopics.notes:
### The rule is about sound, not letters
'i before e except after c' only works for the **long 'ee' sound**. Say the word first, then apply the rule:
- **'ee' sound, no c before it -> ie:** believe, achieve, relieve, retrieve, grief, field, niece, piece, siege, yield, shriek, brief.
- **'ee' sound straight after c -> ei:** receive, deceive, perceive, conceive, ceiling, receipt, deceit, conceit.
- **'ay' sound -> ei:** neighbour, weigh, weight, eight, vein, rein, reign, beige, freight, sleigh.
- **'eye' sound -> ei:** height, sleight, and one pronunciation of either and neither.
Most spelling mistakes come from applying the c-rule to a word that does not have an 'ee' sound.

### When c is followed by ie
Two groups break the simple 'after c' rule, and papers use both:
1. **c sounds 'sh'** — here 'ci' together makes the 'sh' sound, and the e belongs to the next sound: ancient, efficient, sufficient, proficient, deficient, deficiency, conscience, species. Every word ending in **-cient** or **-ciency** is in this group.
2. **i and e are in separate syllables** — sci-ence, so-ci-e-ty, fan-ci-er. The rule only covers ie/ei as one sound.
So 'proficient' is correct and 'proficeint' is wrong, even though the letters come after a c.

### The exceptions worth learning
These have the 'ee' sound (or no clear sound) but still take ei with no c:
- **seize, weird, protein, caffeine, either, neither** — 'ee' sound, ei spelling.
- **leisure, foreign, sovereign, forfeit, counterfeit, heir, their** — ei with other sounds.
- **friend** keeps ie even though it has a short 'e' sound; **mischief** and **sieve** keep ie with a short 'i'.
Learn them as one short list; the rest of the ie/ei words follow the sound rule.

### Words built from a base keep the base spelling
Longer words keep the ie/ei of the base word: achieve -> achievement, relieve -> relief, grieve -> grievance -> grievous, receive -> receipt -> receptionist, deceive -> deceit -> deceitful, perceive -> perception. If you know the short word, you know the long one. Note that 'receipt' also keeps a silent **p** (from Latin *recepta*), which is often dropped.

### How the options are built
Setters usually give four versions of one word:
1. the correct spelling,
2. the ie/ei swap (recieve),
3. the swap plus another slip (reciept),
4. a sound-spelling (receve, retreeve).
Find the ie/ei spot first, check whether a c is right before it, then check the sound. The other slips usually rule themselves out.

### Quick revision
- Say the word: the rule applies only to the 'ee' sound.
- 'ee' sound: ie, except straight after c (receive, ceiling, receipt).
- 'ay' sound -> ei (neighbour, weigh, reign); 'eye' sound -> ei (height).
- c + ie when c sounds 'sh' (ancient, efficient, species) or i and e are separate syllables (science, society).
- Exceptions: seize, weird, protein, caffeine, either, neither, leisure, foreign, sovereign, forfeit, counterfeit, heir, their; friend keeps ie.
- Derived words keep the base: achievement, grievance, deceitful, receipt.

patterns.name: Long 'ee' with no c: ie
patterns.howToSpot: The options differ only in ie/ei and the letter before the pair is not c (achieve, retrieve, grievance, niece).
patterns.logic:
1. Say the word — the pair makes an 'ee' sound.
2. Check the letter before it: not c.
3. Choose ie; reject sound-spellings like 'retreeve'.

*Why it works:* for the 'ee' sound, ie is the default spelling.

example.solution: **Retrieve** — 'ee' sound after r, so ie.

patterns.name: Straight after c: ei
patterns.howToSpot: The ie/ei pair comes directly after a c (receipt, deceit, perceive, ceiling).
patterns.logic:
1. Confirm the c is directly before the pair.
2. Confirm the 'ee' sound (re-CEIPT, de-CEIT).
3. Choose ei, and check for extra letters (the silent p in receipt).

*Why it works:* the 'except after c' part of the rule is reliable for the 'ee' sound.

example.solution: **Receipt** — after c the order is ei, and the silent p stays.

patterns.name: ei exceptions with no c
patterns.howToSpot: The word is from the exception list: seize, weird, foreign, leisure, sovereign, counterfeit, forfeit, protein.
patterns.logic:
1. Recognise the word as an exception.
2. Choose ei even though there is no c.
3. Check the rest of the word (foreigner: -eign-, not -iegn-).

*Why it works:* setters pick these words because the general rule gives the wrong answer.

example.solution: **Seize** — an 'ee' word with ei and no c; it is on the exception list.

patterns.name: c + ie when c sounds 'sh' (-cient, -ciency, species)
patterns.howToSpot: The word has a c followed by ie but the c sounds 'sh' or the i and e are in different syllables: proficient, deficiency, species, society.
patterns.logic:
1. Say the c: is it 'sh' (effi-SHENT) or part of 'sci-ence'?
2. If yes, keep ie after the c.
3. Reject options that force ei after the c (proficeint).

*Why it works:* the c-rule only covers the one-sound 'ee' pair; 'cie' with a 'sh' sound is a different letter group.

example.solution: **Proficient** — c sounds 'sh' (pro-FI-shent), so ie follows c, like efficient and ancient.

subtopics.title: Doubling consonants and one-letter betrayals
subtopics.concept:
**When does the final consonant double before a suffix?** Three conditions, all true:
1. The word ends **consonant–vowel–consonant** (CVC: be**gin**, o**ccur**, re**fer**).
2. The suffix begins with a **vowel** (-ing, -ed, -ance, -ence…).
3. The **stress** falls on that last syllable (be**GIN** → beginning; pre**FER** → preferred).

If stress is elsewhere, no doubling: **BENefit** → benefited (one t), **VISit** → visited, **TARget** → targeted, **ANSwer** → answered.

**Doubling and one-letter traps**

| Correct | Trap spelling | Hook |
|---|---|---|
| **accommodate** | ~~accomodate~~ | room for double c AND double m — the biggest room in spelling |
| **occurrence** | ~~occurence~~ | double c, double r, then -ence |
| **occurred** | ~~occured~~ | occur → occurred: double r, single-ended |
| **committee** | ~~comittee~~ | double m, double t, double e: com-mit-tee |
| **embarrass** | ~~embarass~~ | double r and double s: em-barr-ass |
| **beginning** | ~~begining~~ | be-GIN → beGinning: the g doubles (gin is stressed) |
| **planned** | ~~planed~~ | plan → planned (planed means smoothed wood) |
| **referring** | ~~refering~~ | refer → referring: r doubles |
| **preferred** | ~~prefered~~ | prefer → preferred: r doubles |
| **controlled** | ~~controled~~ | control → controlled: l doubles (British) |
| **benefited** | ~~benifitted~~ | benefit → benefited: only ONE t (stress not on -fit) |
| **targeted** | ~~targetted~~ | target → targeted: ONE t |
| **visited** | ~~vissited~~ | visit → visited: ONE t |
| **answered** | ~~anwsered~~ | answer keeps its w: an-swer-ed |

**The fixed doubles** — words where the doubling is simply part of the word: accommodate (c+m), committee (m+t+e), embarrass (r+s), occurrence/occurred (c+r), millennium (l+n), questionnaire (n), silhouette (t), parallel (one r, double l in the middle, single l at the end).

**Benefited/targeted/visited** are gold: papers plant 'benefitted' and 'targetted' as plausible options, and they are always wrong.

tricks.title: Stress decides doubling
tricks.body: Say the word. If the last syllable is stressed, double before a vowel-suffix (begin→beginning, occur→occurred). If not, don't (benefit→benefited).

tricks.title: Double-double checklist
tricks.body: Five words need TWO doubled letters: accommodate (c,m), committee (m,t), embarrass (r,s), occurrence (c,r), millennium (l,n). Count them.

tricks.title: Letter census
tricks.body: In the options, count the repeated letters. accommodate must show 2 c's and 2 m's; embarrass 2 r's and 2 s's. Eliminate on census failure.

mistakes: Writing 'benefitted' by analogy with 'preferred' — benefit is stress-initial.
One double in 'accommodate' (accomodate / acommodate) — both doubles required.
Writing 'ocurrence' — the c doubles AND the r doubles.
Spelling 'planed' for 'planned' — planed is a different word (smoothed wood).
subtopics.notes:
### Why the consonant doubles
Doubling protects the short vowel. In 'hoping' the single p leaves a long 'o' (hope); in 'hopping' the double p keeps the short 'o' (hop). English applies the same idea to longer words, but only when the **last syllable is stressed**:
- om-**IT** -> omitted, omitting
- re-**GRET** -> regretted, regrettable
- ad-**MIT** -> admitted, admittance
- trans-**FER** -> transferred, transferring
- com-**PEL** -> compelled
- for-**GET** -> forgotten, forgetting

### When the consonant does not double
If the stress is on an earlier syllable, add the suffix directly:
- **DE**-vel-op -> developed, developing
- **BUD**-get -> budgeted
- **PROF**-it -> profited
- **LIM**-it -> limited
- **GAL**-lop -> galloped
- **OF**-fer -> offered; **HAP**-pen -> happened
The consonant also stays single if the word ends in two vowels + consonant (**rain** -> rained, **cool** -> cooled) or two consonants (**help** -> helped), or if the suffix starts with a consonant (**commit** -> commitment, **regret** -> regretful).

### Stress can move
Watch words where the stress shifts in the longer form: re-**FER** -> re-**FERR**-ing, but **REF**-er-ence has only one r; pre-**FER** -> pre-**FERR**-ed, but **PREF**-er-ence and **PREF**-er-able. Say the new word, not the old one.

### Words that simply have double letters
Some doubles have nothing to do with suffixes — they are just part of the word. Learn these by counting:
- **Two or more sets of doubles:** accommodation (cc, mm), possession (ss, ss), address (dd, ss), success (cc, ss), assassinate (ss, ss), committee (mm, tt, ee), embarrass (rr, ss), millennium (ll, nn).
- **One set only:** necessary (one c, double s), recommend (one c, double m), tomorrow (one m, double r), harass (one r, double s), occasion (double c, one s), parallel (one r, double l in the middle, one l at the end), dilemma (one l, double m).

### A letter-count routine
For a double-letter item, write each option's doubles in the margin: necessary = c1 s2; neccessary = c2 s2; necesary = c1 s1. Compare with the pattern you know. This takes about ten seconds and catches mistakes you would miss by just looking at the word.

### British forms in the exam
Indian exams follow British spelling. In British English, words ending in a single vowel + l double the l before a vowel suffix whatever the stress: travel -> travelled, cancel -> cancelled, label -> labelled. American English uses travel -> traveled. If an item offers only one of these as the answer, choose the British form.

### Quick revision
- Double only when the last syllable is stressed and the suffix starts with a vowel: omitted, regrettable, transferred.
- Stress earlier -> no double: developed, budgeted, profited, limited, galloped.
- Say the new word: reference and preference have one r.
- Learn by count: accommodation, possession, address, success; necessary (1 c, 2 s), recommend (1 c, 2 m), tomorrow (1 m, 2 r), harass (1 r, 2 s).
- British: travelled, cancelled, labelled.

patterns.name: Stressed final syllable: double
patterns.howToSpot: A base ending in one vowel + one consonant (omit, regret, transfer) takes -ed, -ing or -able; the options differ in single vs double.
patterns.logic:
1. Say the base word and find the stress: om-IT, re-GRET.
2. If the last syllable is stressed and the suffix starts with a vowel, double the consonant.
3. Do not double any other letter (the m of omit stays single).

*Why it works:* doubling keeps the stressed short vowel short.

example.solution: **Omitted** — stress on -MIT, so the t doubles; the m stays single.

patterns.name: Unstressed final syllable: no double
patterns.howToSpot: The base is stressed on an earlier syllable (DEvelop, BUDget, PROFit) and a double-letter option looks tempting.
patterns.logic:
1. Say the base: DE-vel-op, BUD-get.
2. The stress is not on the last syllable, so add the suffix directly.
3. Reject every option with a doubled final consonant.

*Why it works:* with no stress on the last syllable there is no short vowel to protect.

example.solution: **Developed** — stress on -VEL-, so the p stays single.

patterns.name: Words with two sets of doubles
patterns.howToSpot: The word is from the two-sets list: accommodation, possession, address, success, assassinate.
patterns.logic:
1. Count both sets of doubles: accommodation = cc + mm.
2. Remove any option that has only one set.
3. Check the ending last (-tion, -sion).

*Why it works:* distractors usually keep one double and drop the other, so a quick count finds them.

example.solution: **Possession** — ss + ss; each distractor drops at least one double.

patterns.name: Words with only one double
patterns.howToSpot: The word is often over-doubled: necessary, recommend, tomorrow, harass, occasion.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall which letter doubles: necessary -> s only; recommend -> m only.
2. Remove options that double the wrong letter or both letters.
3. Check the vowels last (necessary, not necessery).

*Why it works:* this group is tested by adding a double where there is none.

example.solution: **Necessary** — one c, double s: 'one collar, two sleeves'.

subtopics.title: -able / -ible, -ance / -ence, -ant / -ent
subtopics.concept:
Three suffix pairs account for a third of SSC spelling items. There is no perfect rule — but there are reliable family anchors:

**-ance vs -ence:** trace the word to its root. persist → persist**ence** (though resist → resist**ance**!). Reliable set: -ence after **fer** (reference, preference, difference, inference), and exist**ence**, independ**ence** (noun) / independ**ent**, depend**ent**, consist**ent**, promin**ent**, magnific**ent**. -ance in: maintain**ance**, appear**ance**, resist**ance**, allegi**ance**, nuis**ance**, hindr**ance** (keep the d), assist**ance**.

**-able vs -ible:** if the stem is a complete word, it is usually -able (comfort-able, accept-able); if the stem is not a word on its own, it is usually -ible (vis-ible, aud-ible, terr-ible). Learn the exceptions as a list: access**ible**, flex**ible**, irresist**ible**. Practical set: feas**ible**, aud**ible**, vis**ible**, terr**ible**, horr**ible**. -able in: notice**able**, change**able**, manage**able** (keep the e!), comfort**able**, accept**able**, remark**able**, avail**able**.

**Suffix families**

| Correct | Trap spelling | Hook |
|---|---|---|
| **independent** | ~~independant~~ | ends -ENT (like dependent, consistent) |
| **dependent** | ~~dependant~~ | ends -ENT (note: 'dependant' is the British noun for a reliant person — SSC prefers dependent in adjectival use) |
| **persistent** | ~~persistant~~ | persist + ent |
| **resistant** | ~~resistent~~ | resist + ant |
| **arrogant** | ~~arrogent~~ | arrog- + ant |
| **prominent** | ~~prominant~~ | promin- + ent |
| **existence** | ~~existance~~ | exist + ence |
| **persistence** | ~~persistense~~ | persist + ence |
| **resistance** | ~~resistence~~ | resist + ance |
| **maintenance** | ~~maintainance~~ | maintain → maintenance (the 'ai' shortens) |
| **appearance** | ~~appearence~~ | appear + ance |
| **allegiance** | ~~allegience~~ | allegi- + ance |
| **nuisance** | ~~nuisence~~ | nuis- + ance |
| **hindrance** | ~~hindrence~~ | keep the d: hindrance (from hinder) |
| **accessible** | ~~accessable~~ | -IBLE after 'cess' |
| **irresistible** | ~~irresistable~~ | -IBLE (re + sist + ible) |
| **feasible** | ~~feasable~~ | -IBLE |
| **noticeable** | ~~noticable~~ | keep the e: notice + able (e saves the soft c) |
| **changeable** | ~~changable~~ | keep the e before -able |
| **manageable** | ~~managable~~ | keep the e |
| **courageous** | ~~couragous~~ | keep the e before -ous |
| **outrageous** | ~~outragous~~ | keep the e |
| **sufficient** | ~~sufficent~~ | -CIENT (like efficient, ancient) |
| **efficient** | ~~efficent~~ | -CIENT |
| **efficient** | ~~efficiant~~ | -CIENT, not -iant |
| **ancient** | ~~anciant~~ | -CIENT |
| **science** | ~~sceince~~ | sci + ence |
| **conscience** | ~~concience~~ | con + science — science is hiding inside |
| **magnificent** | ~~magnificant~~ | -CENT at the end |
| **questionnaire** | ~~questionaire~~ | double n, then -naire (French 'naire') |
| **millennium** | ~~millenium~~ | double l AND double n: mil-lenn-ium |

**Memory economics:** don't learn 'rules' — learn the 30-word families above as units. In the options, the three wrong spellings each break a different letter, so ONE remembered family member settles the item.

tricks.title: Root trace
tricks.body: Strip the suffix and look at the root: exist→exist-ence, maintain→maintenance (ai shortens), resist→resist-ance, persist→persist-ence. The root's own spelling decides.

tricks.title: -fer always -ence
tricks.body: Words from 'fer' nouns take -ence: reference, preference, difference, inference. Verbs keep one f or double by stress: refer→referring, but reference.

tricks.title: Scient family
tricks.body: One family handles four words: sufficient, efficient, ancient, science (and conscience = con + science). All -cient/-ience.

mistakes: Writing 'persistant' by analogy with 'resistant' — the pair split: persist-ence, resist-ance.
Dropping the e in 'noticeable' — the e protects the soft c.
Writing 'maintainance' — maintain's 'ai' shortens to 'e'.
Writing 'magnificant' — it ends -cent.
subtopics.notes:
### Two words people get wrong
The noun from maintain is **maintenance** (never 'maintainance'), and the -ible word meaning 'able to be heard' is **audible** (there is no 'auditible'). Horrible, terrible, visible, audible and feasible all take -ible because their stems (horr-, terr-, vis-, aud-, feas-) are not complete English words.

### -able or -ible: the whole-word test
- If the stem is a **complete word**, the ending is usually **-able**: accept-able, comfort-able, depend-able, remark-able, avail-able, desir(e)-able.
- If the stem is **not a complete word**, the ending is usually **-ible**: poss-ible, horr-ible, vis-ible, cred-ible, ed-ible, plaus-ible, feas-ible.
- A few complete-word stems still take -ible: accessible, flexible, digestible, contemptible, collapsible. Learn these as a short list.
- Many -ible words have a related **-ssion** or **-sion** noun: permission/permissible, division/divisible, comprehension/comprehensible.
- **indispensable** is the most common trap: the stem 'dispense' is a complete word, so it takes -able.

### -ance/-ence and -ant/-ent go together
A word's -ance/-ence noun and its -ant/-ent adjective share the same vowel. Learn one form and you have the other:
- relevant -> relevance; significant -> significance; tolerant -> tolerance; brilliant -> brilliance
- permanent -> permanence; confident -> confidence; obedient -> obedience; coincident -> coincidence
- surveillance, perseverance, maintenance, grievance take -ance (persevere -> perseverance).
When stuck, think of the matching adjective: 'relevent' is wrong because 'relevant' is the adjective.

### Keep or drop the final e
- **Drop the e** before a suffix starting with a vowel: write -> writing, desire -> desirable, argue -> arguing, use -> usable, hope -> hoping.
- **Keep the e** before a suffix starting with a consonant: hope -> hopeful, manage -> management, care -> careful. Exceptions: argue -> argument, true -> truly, nine -> ninth, whole -> wholly.
- **Keep the e after soft c or g** before a or o, so the letter stays soft: notice -> noticeable, change -> changeable, courage -> courageous, advantage -> advantageous, outrage -> outrageous.

### The -y ending
Change y to i after a consonant, keep it after a vowel: happy -> happiness, busy -> business, carry -> carried, but enjoy -> enjoyment, pay -> payable. Keep y before -ing: carrying, studying.

### How to use this in the exam
1. Find the part where the options differ — usually the last four or five letters.
2. Apply one test: whole word? a matching adjective or noun? soft c or g?
3. If no test applies, it is a word you need to know by heart — use the family lists.

### Quick revision
- Complete-word stem -> -able (acceptable, indispensable); non-word stem -> -ible (possible, visible, audible).
- -ssion/-sion noun often signals -ible: permissible, divisible, comprehensible; learn accessible and flexible as exceptions.
- -ance goes with -ant, -ence with -ent: relevant/relevance, permanent/permanence.
- Drop e before a vowel suffix (writing, desirable); keep it after soft c or g (noticeable, advantageous).
- Maintenance, not maintainance; truly, argument, ninth drop the e.

patterns.name: -ance or -ence
patterns.howToSpot: The options differ only in -ance/-ence (perseverance, coincidence, surveillance).
patterns.logic:
1. Think of the matching adjective or verb: coincident -> coincidence.
2. Match the vowel: -ant goes with -ance, -ent with -ence.
3. If there is no matching form, use the word families you know (surveillance, perseverance).

*Why it works:* a noun and its adjective share the same vowel.

example.solution: **Coincidence** — coincident -> coincidence.

patterns.name: -able or -ible
patterns.howToSpot: The options differ in -able/-ible (responsible, indispensable, accessible).
patterns.logic:
1. Remove the ending: is the stem a complete word?
2. Complete word -> -able; not a word -> -ible.
3. Check the -sion clue: permission/permissible, division/divisible.

*Why it works:* -able was added to complete English words; -ible came with Latin stems.

example.solution: **Responsible** — 'respons' is not a complete word, so the ending is -ible.

patterns.name: Keep or drop the final e
patterns.howToSpot: The base ends in e (write, advantage, notice) and the options differ in whether the e stays.
patterns.logic:
1. Does the suffix start with a vowel? Drop the e (writing, desirable).
2. Is there a soft c or g before a or o? Keep the e (advantageous).
3. Consonant suffix: keep the e (management), except truly, argument, ninth.

*Why it works:* the e either marks a long vowel or keeps c and g soft; it goes only when it has no job to do.

example.solution: **Advantageous** — the e keeps the g soft before -ous.

patterns.name: -ant or -ent adjective
patterns.howToSpot: The options differ in -ant/-ent (relevant, permanent, brilliant), usually along with a vowel swap earlier in the word.
patterns.logic:
1. Think of the matching noun: relevance -> relevant, permanence -> permanent.
2. Check the letters before the ending as well (re-LE-vant, per-MA-nent).
3. Remove any option that fails either check.

*Why it works:* the noun keeps the same vowel as the adjective.

example.solution: **Relevant** — relevance -> relevant; 'revelant' also swaps two letters.

subtopics.title: The trap-word bank: silent letters and inherited mistakes
subtopics.concept:
These words are misspelt the same way by lakhs of candidates, which is exactly why examiners choose them. Each carries one hidden letter or one missing letter:

**Trap words**

| Correct | Trap spelling | Hook |
|---|---|---|
| **privilege** | ~~priviledge~~ | no 'd' anywhere: priv-i-lege |
| **rhythm** | ~~rythm~~ | no vowel except y: Rh-y-th-m — 'Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move' |
| **government** | ~~goverment~~ | the n of 'govern' survives: govern + ment |
| **environment** | ~~enviroment~~ | the n of 'environ' survives: environ + ment |
| **separate** | ~~seperate~~ | there's 'a rat' in sePArATE |
| **desperate** | ~~desparate~~ | despERate — it ends -ERate |
| **definite** | ~~definate~~ | ends -INITE (finite inside: def-inite) |
| **definitely** | ~~definately~~ | definite + ly |
| **restaurant** | ~~restaraunt~~ | rest-au-rant: the AU sits in the middle |
| **truly** | ~~truely~~ | true loses its e: tru-ly |
| **argument** | ~~arguement~~ | argue loses its e: argu-ment |
| **ninth** | ~~nineth~~ | nine → ninth: the e drops (but ninety and nineteen keep it) |
| **forty** | ~~fourty~~ | forty has NO u (four does) |
| **publicly** | ~~publically~~ | public + ly — no extra 'al' (unlike tragically) |
| **finally** | ~~fianlly~~ | final + ly: one l in the middle, one at the end |
| **mischievous** | ~~mischevious~~ | ends -VOUS, three syllables: MIS-chi-vous |
| **queue** | ~~queu~~ | q-u-e-u-e: five letters, only Q speaks |
| **vacuum** | ~~vaccum~~ | double u: vac-uum |
| **potato** | ~~potatoe~~ | no e at the end |
| **tomatoes** | ~~tomatos~~ | es after o in the plural |
| **embarrassment** | ~~embarrasment~~ | embarrass + ment keeps both doubles |
| **supersede** | ~~superceed~~ | the only -ede in English: super-sede |
| **proceed** | ~~procede~~ | -CEED: proceed, succeed, exceed |
| **succeed** | ~~suckseed~~ | proceed family |
| **exceed** | ~~excede~~ | proceed family |
| **concede** | ~~concied~~ | -CEDE (different from the -CEED three) |
| **guarantee** | ~~gaurantee~~ | gua first, then rantee |
| **parallel** | ~~paralell~~ | one r, then double l in the middle: p-a-r-a-l-l-e-l |
| **harass** | ~~harrass~~ | ONE r, double s — opposite of embarrass (which has double r) |
| **calendar** | ~~calender~~ | ends -DAR (the machine is a calender; the dates are a calendar) |
| **camaraderie** | ~~comradery~~ | camara- + derie |
| **silhouette** | ~~silohuette~~ | sil-hou-ette: double t |
| **bureaucracy** | ~~buerocracy~~ | bureau + cracy |
| **connoisseur** | ~~conoisseur~~ | double n, -sseur |
| **liaison** | ~~liason~~ | the first i is silent in sound but present in spelling: lia-ison |
| **weird** | ~~wiered~~ | exception word |
| **grateful** | ~~greatful~~ | grate + ful — 'great' is NOT inside it |
| **a lot** | ~~alot~~ | always two words |
| **all right** | ~~alright~~ | formal spelling is two words |
| **skiing** | ~~sking~~ | ski + ing: the i-i collision is correct |
| **radii** | ~~radiuses~~ | plural of radius: radi-i |
| **criterion** | ~~criterias~~ | plural is criteria (no s on criteria) |
| **phenomenon** | ~~phenomenas~~ | plural is phenomena |
| **stimulus** | ~~stimuluses~~ | plural is stimuli |
| **analysis** | ~~analysises~~ | plural is analyses |
| **crisis** | ~~crisises~~ | plural is crises |
| **cactus** | ~~cactuses~~ | classical plural is cacti |

**Groups inside the bank:**
- **Silent letters preserved:** government (n), environment (n), rhythm (no vowel but y), queue, vacuum (uu), liaison (i), silhouette (t,h).
- **Missing-letter classics:** truly (no e), argument (argue drops e), ninth (nine drops e), forty (no u), publicly (no 'al'), definite (not -ate).
- **Foreign borrowings:** restaurant (au), guarantee (gua), bureaucracy (eau), connoisseur, camaraderie, questionnaire, millennium.
- **-ceed vs -cede:** only THREE words take -ceed: proceed, succeed, exceed. Everything else takes -cede: concede, recede, precede. And one loner: **supersede** is the only -sede in English.
- **Plurals:** criteria (not criterias), phenomena (not phenomenas), stimuli, analyses, crises — plural already means many; adding s doubles it wrongly.

Revise this bank weekly; it is the single highest-yield page in the topic.

tricks.title: The n-test for -ment words
tricks.body: government = govern+ment, environment = environ+ment: the root's final n must survive. Ask 'what is the root?' — the letter reappears.

tricks.title: Three -ceed, one -sede
tricks.body: proceed, succeed, exceed = the only -ceed words; supersede = the only -sede. All other 'seed-sound' words are -cede.

tricks.title: No- doubling plurals
tricks.body: criteria, phenomena, stimuli, data already are plurals — any option adding -s to them is instantly wrong.

mistakes: Writing 'gaurantee' — swap of a and u; gua-rantee.
Writing 'greatful' — grate + ful; 'great' is not in the word.
Writing 'alot' — it is always two words: a lot.
Writing 'calender' for the date-chart — the machine spelling.
subtopics.notes:
### Three words to look at closely
- **parallel** has **one r** and a **double l in the middle**, with a single l at the end: p-a-r-a-l-l-e-l.
- **skiing** is right (ski + ing); the only misspelling tested is 'sking'.
- **ninth**: nine drops its e before -th (ninth), but keeps it in **ninety** and **nineteen**.
Also, **cacti** and **cactuses** are both accepted plurals, and both **collectable** and **collectible** are standard. Neither of these should be the only answer in an item.

### Silent letters
Many trap words have a letter you do not pronounce:
- **Silent p:** psychology, pneumonia, receipt, cupboard, raspberry.
- **Silent d:** Wednesday, handkerchief, grandson.
- **Silent b:** debt, doubt, subtle, plumber, tomb.
- **Silent h:** rhythm, rhyme, exhaust, exhibition, ghost.
- **Silent s:** island, aisle, debris.
- **Silent n after m:** autumn, column, condemn, solemn.
Say the word slowly the way it is spelt (WED-NES-DAY) to remember the silent letter.

### -ceed, -cede and -sede
- **-ceed:** only proceed, succeed, exceed (and their forms: proceedings, succeeded, exceeding).
- **-sede:** only supersede.
- **-cede:** every other word — precede, recede, concede, secede, intercede.
Also note the vowel change in the related words: proceed -> **procedure** and succeed -> **success** keep the c but not the double e.

### When a root word changes its letters
- **pronounce -> pronunciation** — the o after 'pron' disappears (pro-NUN-ci-a-tion).
- **explain -> explanation**, **maintain -> maintenance**, **exclaim -> exclamation** — ai becomes a or e.
- **curious -> curiosity**, **generous -> generosity** — the u disappears.
- **four -> forty** (but fourteen), **nine -> ninth**.
- **argue -> argument**, **true -> truly**, **due -> duly**.
Remember these as pairs; the exam usually offers a spelling that keeps the root unchanged.

### Borrowed words
French and Latin borrowings keep their original spelling:
- **entrepreneur** (entre + pre + neur), **bureaucracy** (bureau + cracy), **connoisseur**, **rendezvous**, **reservoir**, **silhouette**, **camaraderie**, **liaison**, **questionnaire**.
Break them into parts: bureau + cracy, entre + pre + neur. The common mistake is to swap letters within a part ('entreprenuer').

### Quick revision
- Silent letters: psychology, Wednesday, subtle, rhythm, island, autumn.
- Only proceed, succeed and exceed end in -ceed; only supersede ends in -sede; everything else ends in -cede.
- Root changes: pronunciation, explanation, forty, ninth, argument, truly.
- Borrowed words: learn by parts (bureau + cracy, entre + pre + neur).
- Parallel = one r, double l in the middle.

patterns.name: Silent letter
patterns.howToSpot: The word contains a letter you do not pronounce (Wednesday, psychology, subtle) and one or more options leave it out.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the silent letter by saying the word as it is spelt (WED-NES-DAY).
2. Remove every option that drops it.
3. Check the order of the remaining letters.

*Why it works:* the most common mistake is to spell the word the way it sounds.

example.solution: **Wednesday** — Wed + nes + day; the d is silent but written.

patterns.name: -ceed, -cede or -sede
patterns.howToSpot: The options differ in -ceed / -cede / -sede, or in the vowel before it (precede, succeeded, exceed).
patterns.logic:
1. Is it proceed, succeed or exceed? Then -ceed.
2. Is it supersede? Then -sede.
3. Otherwise -cede.

*Why it works:* the list of exceptions is only four words long.

example.solution: **Precede** — not one of the three -ceed words, so -cede.

patterns.name: Root letter changed in the longer word
patterns.howToSpot: The word comes from a root that changes its letters: pronounce -> pronunciation, nine -> ninth, four -> forty.
patterns.logic:
1. Think of the root and how it changes.
2. Remove the option that keeps the root unchanged (pronounciation, nineth).
3. Check the remaining options letter by letter.

*Why it works:* the most common wrong option keeps the root word as it is.

example.solution: **Pronunciation** — the o of pronounce disappears: pro-nun-ci-a-tion.

patterns.name: Borrowed word
patterns.howToSpot: A French or Latin borrowing: entrepreneur, bureaucracy, connoisseur, rendezvous, silhouette.
patterns.logic:
1. Split the word into parts: bureau + cracy.
2. Check each part in each option.
3. Remove options with swapped letters inside a part (entreprenuer).

*Why it works:* borrowed words keep their original spelling, so checking part by part is reliable.

example.solution: **Bureaucracy** — bureau + cracy.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy: how to judge a spelling you have never seen
subtopics.concept:
The item shows four spellings of one word and asks for the correct one. Even when the word is unfamiliar, four elimination moves settle most items:

1. **Find the difference.** Scan the four options letter by letter; they differ in one or two spots (recie-ve / recei-ve / rece-ve). Concentrate only on the differing spot.
2. **Apply the rule that spot obeys.** c before the pair → ei. Root -fer → -ence noun. CVC stressed → doubling. If no rule applies, it is a bank word — the weekly bank revision answers it.
3. **Say each option.** The mouth knows rhythm: 'mis-CHEE-vious' (4 syllables) is wrong because mischievous has 3.
4. **Syllable-split check.** Split into syllables and confirm no letter is missing or doubled: res-tau-rant → rest-au-rant needs the au.

**Daily plan (15 minutes):** 10 new bank words + rewrite yesterday's 10 from memory, marking every miss. Self-dictation — write sentences containing bank words, then re-check spelling a day later — converts seeing into spelling.

**In the exam:** 25–35 seconds. Most SSC spelling items are bank words; the rest yield to the c-test and the stress rule. Never leave it blank — there is no penalty pattern that favours skipping over one informed guess among four.

tricks.title: Difference-first reading
tricks.body: Don't read four full words — read the one letter-position where they differ. Options are built to differ in a single spot; that spot is the entire question.

tricks.title: Syllable count
tricks.body: Count syllables: mischievous (3), restaurant (2-3 as res-tau-rant), rhythm (2). A wrong spelling often forces a syllable that cannot be pronounced.

tricks.title: Write-from-memory drill
tricks.body: Recognition is not recall. Cover the bank, write the words, mark misses, repeat tomorrow — misses halve each cycle.

mistakes: Choosing the option that 'looks nicer' — options are engineered so the wrong one looks smoother.
Skipping letter-by-letter comparison; one letter is the whole item.
Ignoring AmE/BrE traps — SSC follows British spelling, so favour travelled/colour/centre forms when they appear.
Guessing on bank words instead of trusting the weekly revision — these are the free marks.
subtopics.notes:
### Three question types
1. **Choose the correct spelling** — four versions of one word. Compare the options letter by letter and focus on the spot where they differ.
2. **Find the misspelt word** — four different words, one of them wrong. Here you cannot compare options, so check each word against what you know: its doubles, its ie/ei, its ending, any silent letters.
3. **Misspelt word in a sentence** — the same as type 2, but the words are inside a sentence. Ignore the meaning and check each listed word on its own.
A fourth type asks for a **plural or related form** (criterion -> criteria). This depends on knowing classical plurals.

### Checking a word you cannot compare
For type 2 and type 3 items, run four quick checks on each word:
1. **Doubles:** does it have the right double letters? (tomorrow: 1 m, 2 r; harass: 1 r, 2 s)
2. **ie/ei:** does the pair follow the sound rule? (achievement)
3. **Ending:** -ance/-ence, -able/-ible, -ceed/-cede?
4. **Silent or dropped letters:** Wednesday, government, pronunciation.
The misspelt word usually fails one check clearly. If three words pass easily, the fourth is the answer even if you are unsure of it.

### Classical plurals
Latin and Greek nouns keep their original plurals:
- **-on -> -a:** criterion -> criteria, phenomenon -> phenomena.
- **-is -> -es:** crisis -> crises, analysis -> analyses, thesis -> theses, basis -> bases.
- **-us -> -i:** stimulus -> stimuli, radius -> radii, nucleus -> nuclei.
- **-um -> -a:** medium -> media, datum -> data, curriculum -> curricula.
Adding -s to these plurals (criterias, crisises) is always wrong.

### Long words: split them into syllables
For long words like conscientious, miscellaneous or unnecessary, write the syllables and check each one:
- con-sci-en-tious (con + science + tious)
- mis-cel-la-ne-ous (double l, then -aneous)
- un-ne-ces-sa-ry (un + necessary: two n's where the prefix meets the word)
Prefixes do not change the root: un + necessary = unnecessary, mis + spell = misspell, dis + satisfied = dissatisfied. The double letter where the prefix meets the root is a common test.

### Time and guessing
A spelling item should take 20-30 seconds. If you are unsure between two options, choose the one that follows a rule (sound rule, stress rule, whole-word rule) over the one that simply looks familiar — setters often write the wrong option to look natural.

### Quick revision
- Choose-the-correct: compare the options at the one spot where they differ.
- Find-the-misspelt: check doubles, ie/ei, ending and silent letters for each word.
- Classical plurals: criteria, phenomena, crises, analyses, stimuli, radii, media — never add -s.
- Long words: split into syllables; prefix + root keeps both letters (unnecessary, misspell).
- Unsure between two: pick the one that follows a rule.

patterns.name: Find the misspelt word (four different words)
patterns.howToSpot: The four options are different words and the question asks which one is spelt wrongly.
patterns.logic:
1. Check each word against its known signature: doubles, ie/ei, ending, silent letters.
2. Mark the words that pass clearly.
3. The one that fails is the answer.

*Why it works:* three words are correct, so one clear failure decides the item.

example.solution: **Tommorow** is wrong — tomorrow has one m and double r.

patterns.name: Misspelt word inside a sentence
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence is given and the options are four words from it; one is misspelt.
patterns.logic:
1. Ignore the meaning of the sentence.
2. Check each option on its own, as in a find-the-misspelt item.
3. Do not be distracted by British forms such as recognised — these are correct.

*Why it works:* the sentence is only a setting; the test is still one word.

example.q: The comittee will announce its decision on Wednesday. Options: comittee / announce / decision / Wednesday
example.solution: **comittee** is wrong — committee has double m, double t, double e.

patterns.name: Classical plural
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the plural of a Latin or Greek noun (criterion, crisis, analysis, phenomenon).
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the ending: -on, -is, -us, -um.
2. Apply the classical change: -on -> -a, -is -> -es, -us -> -i, -um -> -a.
3. Reject any option that adds -s to the plural.

*Why it works:* these words keep their original plurals in formal English.

example.q: Plural of crisis: crises / crisises / crisis / crisies
example.solution: **crises** — -is becomes -es.

patterns.name: Long word: check syllable by syllable
patterns.howToSpot: A long word (conscientious, miscellaneous, unnecessary) with options that differ at one or two places.
patterns.logic:
1. Split the word into syllables.
2. Check each syllable in each option, especially where a prefix meets the root.
3. The option with every syllable correct is the answer.

*Why it works:* long words are hard to take in at a glance, but each syllable is easy to check.

example.solution: **Unnecessary** — un + necessary: double n at the join, one c, double s.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Four spellings of one word; find the correct one.
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the differing letter-spot, apply the relevant rule (c-test, stress-doubling, suffix family), else recall from the bank.

example.q: Select the correctly spelt word: Accommodation / Accomodation / Acommodation / Accommodasion
example.solution: Accommodation — the options differ only in the doubles; the word needs both cc and mm.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Four different words are given; one of them is misspelt.
pyqPatterns.approach: Check each word against its doubles, ie/ei pair, ending and silent letters. Three pass; the one that fails is the answer.

example.q: Select the wrongly spelt word: Existance / Occasion / Believe / Truly
example.solution: Existance — exist goes with existent, so the noun is existence.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sentence is given and four of its words are the options; one is misspelt.
pyqPatterns.approach: Ignore the meaning and check each listed word on its own. British forms (colour, organised) are correct in Indian exams.

example.q: The committee could not reach a concensus on the budget.
example.solution: concensus -> consensus (related to consent).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the plural of a Latin or Greek noun, or for a derived form of a given word.
pyqPatterns.approach: Classical plurals: -on -> -a, -is -> -es, -us -> -i, -um -> -a. Never add -s to a plural that is already classical (criterias).

example.solution: analyses — -is becomes -es, as in crisis -> crises.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options differ only in the order of i and e.
pyqPatterns.approach: Say the word. 'ee' sound: ie, but ei straight after c. 'ay' sound: ei. Check the exception list (seize, weird, foreign, leisure). c sounding 'sh' keeps ie (efficient, species).

example.solution: Perceive — the 'ee' pair follows c, so ei.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options differ in whether the last consonant of the base is doubled before -ed, -ing, -able or -ance.
pyqPatterns.approach: Double only if the last syllable of the base is stressed and the suffix starts with a vowel: regrettable, forgotten. Otherwise do not: budgeted, galloped.

example.solution: Budgeted — the stress is on BUD-, so the t stays single.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options differ only in the last few letters.
pyqPatterns.approach: Match -ance with -ant and -ence with -ent; complete-word stems take -able; drop a final e before a vowel suffix except after soft c or g (noticeable).

example.solution: Perseverance — persevere + ance, with one r.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The word has a silent letter (Wednesday, psychology) or ends in the 'seed' sound.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the silent letter by saying the word as spelt. Only proceed, succeed and exceed end in -ceed; only supersede ends in -sede; the rest end in -cede.

example.solution: Supersede — the only -sede verb.

solvedExamples.solution: The word from 'occur' doubles **both** c and r and ends **-ence**: occurrence. Census: two c's, two r's. Occurence (one r), Occurrance (-ance), Ocurrence (one c) all fail.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Census test: occur → cc + rr + ence.

solvedExamples.solution: Privilege has **no d** and **no double l**: priv-i-lege. The 'd' in 'priviledge' is the classic planted error — there is no 'd' sound in careful speech either.
solvedExamples.shortcut: No-d test: privilege contains no letter d at all.

solvedExamples.solution: From 'maintain', the **'ai' shortens to 'e'** and the ending is **-ance**: maintenance. So Maintainance (keeps ai), Maintenence (-ence), Maintanance (drops the i) are all wrong.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Root trace: maintain → maintenance (ai → e, end -ance).

practice.solution: Embarrass carries **double r and double s** — em-barr-ass. Each distractor drops exactly one of the doubles.
practice.shortcut: Double-double word: r and s both doubled.

practice.solution: Rhythm has **no vowel except y**: Rh-y-th-m. Mnemonic: Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move. Rhythem plants a fake e; Rythm drops the h.
Independent ends **-ent** (same family as dependent, consistent, persistent). Every distractor swaps the final vowel pair.
Committee doubles **m, t and e**: com-mit-tee. The census needs mm, tt, ee — only the fourth option shows all three.
Separate: remember there is **'a rat' in sePArATE** — the middle vowel is a, not e. This is the most-failed word in the bank.
From French questionnaire: **double n** and the ending **-naire**. Questionaire loses an n; Questionnair drops the final e.
The **-cient family**: sufficient, efficient, ancient. The spelling needs ff + ie + nt.
Millennium doubles **l and n**: mil-lenn-ium (from Latin mille + annus). The distractors each drop or move one double.
Desperate ends **-perate**: desp-ER-ate. 'Desparate' (the common swap to -ara-) is the planted error.
Restaurant = **rest-au-rant**: the 'au' sits between rest and rant. Restaraunt reverses to 'ar'; Restauraunt adds a phantom u.
Mischievous has **three syllables** (MIS-chi-vous) and ends **-vous**. Mischevious/mischievious insert an extra syllable — the classic error.
Keep the **e** before -able: noticeable. The e protects the soft 'c' sound (notice → notice-able). Noticable is the planted drop.
practice.shortcut: Keep-e rule: soft c needs its e.

practice.solution: Occurrence: double c, double r, **-ence** ending. Occurance/Ocurrance take -ance; Occurence drops an r.
The root **govern** keeps its n before -ment: government. Dropping the n is the single most common misspelling in this family.
True drops its final e before -ly: **truly** (like duly). Truely keeps a phantom e; Truelly doubles an l that was never there.
**Achievement** = achieve + ment. The pair makes an 'ee' sound after h (not c), so it is **ie**, and the e of achieve stays before the consonant suffix -ment.
practice.shortcut: No c before the 'ee' pair -> ie; achieve keeps its e.

practice.solution: **Grievance** comes from grieve: 'ee' sound after r, so **ie**. The e of grieve drops before the vowel suffix, and the ending is -ance: griev + ance.
**Hygiene** is pronounced HY-jeen: an 'ee' sound after g, not c, so the pair is **ie**. The word ends in a single n and a final e.
**Perceive** — the 'ee' pair comes straight after c, so it is **ei**, like receive and deceive. The c must stay; 'persieve' replaces it with s.
**Deceitful** = deceit + ful. After c the 'ee' pair is **ei** (deceive, deceit), and the suffix -ful always has one l.
**Conceited** comes from conceit: the 'ee' pair follows c, so it is **ei**. The c must stay, which rules out 'consieted'.
**Weird** is one of the exceptions: an 'ee'-type sound with **ei** and no c before it. Learn it with seize, protein and caffeine.
practice.shortcut: Exception list: weird, seize, protein -> ei.

practice.solution: **Counterfeit** ends in -feit, like forfeit; both are on the ei exception list. The first part is 'counter', spelt as the ordinary word.
**Sovereignty** = sovereign + ty. Sovereign ends in -eign, like foreign and reign, so the pair is **ei**. The suffix is -ty, not -ity.
**Species** is said SPEE-sheez: the c sounds 'sh', so 'ci' belongs together and the word is spelt **-cies**, even though the letters come after a c.
**Deficiency** follows deficient: the c sounds 'sh' (de-FI-shen-see), so the letters are **-ciency**, like efficiency and proficiency. The f is single.
practice.shortcut: Every -ciency word keeps ie after c.

practice.solution: **Conscientious** = con + science + tious. Science is inside the word, so the letters after sc are **-ie-**; the ending is -tious with the u.
practice.shortcut: con + scien + tious: science is hiding inside.

practice.solution: **Regrettable**: re-GRET is stressed on its last syllable and -able starts with a vowel, so the t doubles. The g stays single, and the ending is -able because 'regret' is a complete word.
**Forgotten**: for-GOT is stressed on its last syllable, so the t doubles before -en. The ending is -en, not -on.
**Budgeted**: BUD-get is stressed on the first syllable, so the final t does not double before -ed. The d before g is single.
practice.shortcut: Stress on BUD- -> no double t.

practice.solution: **Galloped**: GAL-lop is stressed on the first syllable, so the p stays single. The double l is part of the base word gallop.
**Accommodation** has two doubles: **cc** and **mm**. Each distractor drops one of them or changes the -tion ending.
**Assassination** = ass + ass + ination: **ss** twice, then -tion. Distractors drop one ss or change the ending.
**Recommend** = re + commend: one c, double m. Only the m of 'commend' is doubled.
practice.shortcut: re + commend -> one c, two m.

practice.solution: **Harassment** = harass + ment: one r, double s. It is the opposite of embarrass, which doubles both r and s.
**Obedience** goes with the adjective obedient, so the noun ends in **-ence**. The vowels are o-be-di-ence.
**Perseverance** = persevere + ance: the e of persevere drops before the vowel suffix, and the ending is **-ance**. The r is single.
**Surveillance** is a French borrowing: sur + veill + ance. It keeps **-eill-** with double l and ends in **-ance**.
**Permissible**: the stem 'permiss' is not a complete word, and the related noun is permission, so the ending is **-ible**. The s is doubled, as in permission.
**Dependable** = depend + able. 'Depend' is a complete word, so the ending is **-able**.
**Guidance** = guide + ance. The final e of guide drops before a suffix that starts with a vowel, and the ending is -ance. The word starts gu-i, as in guide.
practice.shortcut: Drop e before a vowel suffix: guid + ance.

practice.solution: **Pronounceable** = pronounce + able. The e stays because it keeps the c soft before a, just as in noticeable. The ending is -able because pronounce is a complete word.
practice.shortcut: Soft c before -able keeps the e.

practice.solution: **Permanent** goes with the noun permanence, so the adjective ends in **-ent**. The vowels are per-ma-nent.
**Significant** goes with the noun significance, so the adjective ends in **-ant**. The f is single and the n after g must stay.
**Psychology** starts with a silent p (psych-) and keeps the h after c: p-s-y-c-h.
**Handkerchief** = hand + kerchief. The d of hand is silent but written, and kerchief ends in **-chief**, spelt exactly like the word chief (ie).
**Succeeded**: succeed is one of the three -ceed verbs (proceed, succeed, exceed), so it keeps **-ceed** before -ed. It also has double c.
**Supersede** is the only English verb ending in **-sede**. Neither -seed, -sead nor -ceed is correct.
**Explanation**: the ai of explain becomes a single **a** in the noun (ex-pla-na-tion). Keeping the root unchanged gives the common error 'explaination'.
**Curiosity**: the u of curious drops in the noun (cu-ri-os-i-ty), as in generous -> generosity.
**Entrepreneur** = entre + pre + neur, from French. The ending is **-eur** (like connoisseur), and there is an r after the second p.
**Rendezvous** is French: rendez + vous. Both the z and the final s are silent but written.
practice.shortcut: rendez + vous: z and s both silent.

practice.solution: **Begining** is wrong: be-GIN is stressed, so the n doubles — **beginning**. Receive (c + ei), calendar (-dar) and grateful (grate + ful) are correct.
**Existance** is wrong: it goes with existent, so it is **existence**. Occasion (cc, one s), believe (ie) and truly (true drops e) are correct.
**Liason** is wrong: the word is **liaison**, with an i on both sides of the a (li-ai-son). Guarantee, vacuum and silhouette are correct.

practice.q:
Identify the misspelt word in the following sentence.

*The government has recieved several complaints about the new tax.*
practice.solution: **recieved** is wrong: after c the 'ee' pair is ei — **received**. Government (govern + ment), several and complaints are correct.

practice.q:
Identify the misspelt word in the following sentence.

*Her sudden dissappearance puzzled the entire village.*
practice.solution: **dissappearance** is wrong: dis + appear + ance gives one s and double p — **disappearance**. Sudden, puzzled and entire are correct.
practice.shortcut: dis + appear: one s, two p.

practice.q:
Identify the misspelt word in the following sentence.

*The committee could not reach a concensus on the budget.*
practice.solution: **concensus** is wrong: the word is **consensus** (related to consent), with s in both places. Committee (mm, tt, ee), reach and budget are correct.
**criteria** — Greek nouns in -on take -a in the plural (criterion -> criteria, phenomenon -> phenomena). Criteria is already plural, so 'criterias' is wrong.
**phenomena** — -on becomes -a. Adding -s to phenomena, or using the Latin -ae or -um endings, is wrong.
**analyses** — nouns in -is change to -es in the plural (crisis -> crises, thesis -> theses). 'analysis' is the singular, and the other forms do not exist.
**Miscellaneous** = mis-cel-la-ne-ous: sc, double l, then -aneous (as in simultaneous).
**Misspell** = mis + spell. The prefix does not change the root, so the s of mis and the s of spell both stay, and spell keeps its double l.
practice.shortcut: Prefix + root keeps both letters: mis + spell.

practice.solution: **Dissatisfied** = dis + satisfied: double s where the prefix meets the root, then satisfy -> satisfied (y after a consonant becomes i).
practice.shortcut: dis + satisfied: ss at the join.
